newsitem.title: USA: China official says Hong Kong can run phones.
newsitem.headline: China official says Hong Kong can run phones.

text.p: China will allow Hong Kong to operate its own telecommunications network after China takes over the British colony next summer, a Chinese telecommunications official said on Wednesday.

"After the return of Hong Kong to mainland China in 1997 their local telecommunications services will be totally administered and controlled under Hong Kong administration," Liu Cai, the director general of policy and regulation at China's Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications, said.

"So our central government will not interfere in their administration of local telecommunications," Liu said. He spoke through a translator at a conference in Washington sponsored by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies.

Liu said his ministry, which regulates telecommunications in China, was not opposed to the government-controlled network China Telecom participating in the Hong Kong market, but that officials thought it better for China Telecom not to participate "too much."
China takes over Hong Kong in July next year after 155 years of British rule.
Liu said that in the last five years China's telecommunications network had enjoyed an average annual growth rate of 51 percent. Still, he said, just 6 percent of the population had a telephone.

Over the next four years China hopes to double the size of its telephone network, with much of the new equipment coming from foreign providers, he said. "Of course this new generation of technlogy will need to cooperate with foreign companies, espcially American companies."
China intends to pass a new telecommunications law by the end of 1997 or the beginning of 1998 to provide a legal framework for its expanding network, Liu said.

But the law was not expected to deal with the question of getting the government out of the telephone business. Liu said a government monopoly was still needed to speed construction of China's telephone network. Ultimately this could change "step by step," he said, but offered no timetable.

Liu said it was unclear whether the new telecommunications law would address the issue of restrictions on foreign ownership in the telecommunications sector, but said his ministry was studying the issue. "We are currently considering using foreign investment in a more open way."
Asked whether his ministry would be regulating Internet access in China, Liu said, "I think it (decisions about Internet access) will be done more at political levels."
